gloss: A figure showing the size, length, or amount of something.
examples: Take a *measurement* before you cut the board.

gloss: A unit or standard used to state size or amount.

gloss: A fixed amount used as a standard for measuring.

gloss: How large or small something is.

gloss: The measurement of something from one end to the other.

The pool is fifty meters in *length*.
Cut two *lengths* of rope the same size.

gloss: The measurement of something from one side to the other.

The fabric comes in two *widths*.

gloss: How deep something is from the top down.

gloss: How thick something is from one surface to the other.

gloss: The amount of space between two places or things.

He can throw a football a good *distance*.
They drove long *distances* every weekend.

countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
gloss: How heavy something is, or a heavy object used for lifting or holding something down.

Put a *weight* on the papers so they don't blow away.

gloss: The amount of matter in an object, measured in kilograms.

gloss: The amount of space that something fills.

Water expands in *volume* when it freezes.
The tank holds a large *volume* of fuel.

gloss: The amount that a container or a space can hold.

The two coolers have different *capacities*.

gloss: The size of a flat surface, found by multiplying length by width.

Add the *areas* of the two rooms together.

gloss: How fast something moves.
examples: Cut your *speed* on the wet road.
The train reaches *speeds* of 150 miles an hour.
He read the whole book at record *speed*.

gloss: Speed in a particular direction, used in science.

They measured the bullet's *velocity*.
Wind *velocities* were highest near the coast.

gloss: The speed at which someone walks, runs, or works.

He walked at a steady *pace*.
The runners hit very different *paces* in the last mile.

gloss: How fast something happens, measured against time or another amount.

Interest *rates* went up again.

The *amount* of rain this spring was unusual.
Large *amounts* of data were lost.

gloss: How much of something there is.

The recipe lists the *quantity* of each ingredient.

gloss: A measurement such as length, width, or height.
examples: Give me the *dimensions* of the room.
The new box has the same *dimensions* as the old one.
Height is the third *dimension*.

gloss: How much mass a material has for its size.
examples: Lead has a much higher *density* than aluminum.
Oil floats on water because of its lower *density*.
The lab measured the *density* of each sample.

gloss: A push or a pull acting on an object, measured in newtons.
examples: The *force* of the wind snapped the branch.
Two *forces* act on the box at the same time.
Apply a steady *force* to the lever.

gloss: An amount stated as a part of a hundred.
examples: A high *percentage* of the class passed.
What *percentage* of your income goes to rent?
The two *percentages* don't add up to a hundred.

gloss: One part in a hundred.
examples: About twenty *percent* of the crop was lost.
Only a few *percent* of applicants get in.
Sales rose ten *percent* last quarter.
contrast: Americans write it as one word, percent; the British write per cent. The plural is percent, never percents.

gloss: A part of a whole, such as one half or three quarters.
examples: Add the two *fractions* and reduce the answer.
The repair cost a *fraction* of what I expected.
Only a small *fraction* of the seeds came up.

gloss: A number written with a point, such as 0.75.
examples: Round the *decimal* to two places.
Turn the fraction into a *decimal*.
The chart lists everything in *decimals*.
contrast: Americans write a decimal point where Russian uses a comma: 3.5, not 3,5.

gloss: The result of adding numbers together and dividing by how many there are.
examples: The *average* of the five scores is eighty-two.
Rainfall was above *average* this month.
Their batting *averages* were nearly identical.

gloss: The average of a set of numbers.
examples: Report the *mean* along with the range.
The *mean* and the median are far apart here.
Both *means* came out close to fifty.
contrast: The same spelling is also the verb to mean and the adjective mean, unkind.

gloss: The middle value in a list of numbers arranged in order.
examples: The *median* tells you more than the average here.
Half the houses sold above the *median*.
The two *medians* were identical.
contrast: In American English the same word also names the strip in the middle of a highway.

gloss: A part of a whole, compared with the rest.
examples: A large *proportion* of the budget goes to salaries.
Mix the paint in the right *proportion*.
The *proportions* of sand and cement matter a lot.

gloss: How close a measurement is to the true value.
examples: The scale loses *accuracy* when it's cold.
We double-checked the numbers for *accuracy*.
GPS gives *accuracy* within a few feet.

gloss: The level of fine detail that a measurement is made to.
examples: The part was machined with great *precision*.
Lab work demands *precision*.
You don't need that much *precision* for a garden fence.

gloss: The amount a measurement is allowed to vary from the exact figure.
examples: The part is machined to a *tolerance* of one thousandth of an inch.
That's outside the *tolerance* on the drawing.
Aerospace parts have very tight *tolerances*.

gloss: An extra amount allowed beyond what is strictly needed.
examples: Leave a *margin* of error in your estimate.
He won by a *margin* of two seconds.
The *margins* on this drawing are too tight.

gloss: One of the equal steps by which something increases.
examples: The dial moves in five-degree *increments*.
Raise the temperature by a small *increment*.
You can pay it off in monthly *increments*.

gloss: The space or time between two points.
examples: Take a reading at five-minute *intervals*.
There was a long *interval* between the two flashes.
The posts are set at even *intervals*.

gloss: The adjusting of an instrument so that its readings are correct.
examples: The scale is due for *calibration*.
*Calibration* takes about ten minutes.
Poor *calibration* explains the strange readings.

gloss: A figure shown by a measuring instrument.
examples: The meter *reading* was higher than last month.
Take a *reading* every hour.
Both *readings* came out the same.

gloss: The amount of a medicine to be taken and how often.
examples: Follow the *dosage* on the label.
The doctor lowered his *dosage*.
Children's *dosages* are based on weight.

gloss: A small part taken from something so that it can be tested.
examples: The lab tested a water *sample* from the well.
Take a *sample* from the middle of the batch.
All three *samples* came back clean.
contrast: Americans say SAM-puhl with a short a; the British say SAHM-puhl.

gloss: A standard figure that other results are compared against.
examples: That test sets the *benchmark* for the industry.
Our numbers are below the national *benchmark*.
They ran the same *benchmarks* on both machines.

gloss: An agreed level or measure that things are judged against.
examples: The meter is the international *standard* of length.
This part doesn't meet the *standard*.
Safety *standards* have gotten stricter.

gloss: A number used to measure how well something is doing.
examples: Response time is the *metric* we watch.
Pick one *metric* and track it all year.
The dashboard shows a dozen *metrics*.

gloss: The size or strength of something, especially on a scientific scale.

Nobody grasped the *magnitude* of the problem.
The two stars differ by three *magnitudes*.

gloss: How large something is or how far it reaches.

The full *extent* of the flooding wasn't clear until morning.

gloss: The greatest amount that is allowed or possible.

There's a *limit* to how much that shelf will hold.
Both weight *limits* were raised last year.

gloss: The weight carried or supported by something.

Heavy *loads* wear out the springs.

gloss: Large size or volume, especially when it makes something hard to handle.

gloss: The total number found by counting.

The two *counts* didn't match.

Their *tallies* were off by three.

gloss: The amount you get when everything is added together.

The monthly *totals* are on the last page.

gloss: A figure that is close to the true one but not exact.

gloss: A value showing what share of a group falls below it.

The chart is divided into *percentiles*.

gloss: A number, especially one in a report or a set of results.

Check the *figures* one more time.

gloss: Any one of the symbols from 0 to 9.

gloss: An American unit of length equal to 2.54 centimeters.

gloss: One hundredth of a meter.

gloss: One thousandth of a meter.

gloss: One thousand meters, a little over six tenths of a mile.

The border is a *kilometer* from here.
Road signs in Canada are in *kilometers*.

gloss: The number of miles a vehicle has traveled, or how far it goes on a gallon of fuel.
examples: The car has low *mileage* for its age.

Check the *mileage* before you buy it.

gloss: A length or an area measured in feet.

gloss: The distance from one end of something to the other.

gloss: The total distance around the edge of a shape or an area.

gloss: A unit of water depth equal to six feet.

gloss: The distance around something thick, such as a tree or a waist.

gloss: The distance across something from one side to the other.

gloss: The scientific unit of temperature, counted up from absolute zero.

gloss: The temperature at which a liquid turns to vapor.

gloss: The temperature at which a liquid turns solid.

gloss: The gauge in a vehicle that shows how fast it is going.

Older *speedometers* were driven by a cable.

gloss: The instrument in a vehicle that records the total miles traveled.

My watch has a built-in *altimeter*.
Both *altimeters* read the same.

A *micrometer* reads down to a thousandth of an inch.
The shop keeps three *micrometers* in the drawer.

gloss: A tool with two adjustable arms for measuring thickness or diameter.
examples: Measure the bolt with a *caliper*.

gloss: A flat half-circle marked in degrees, used for measuring angles.

The *protractors* were still in the box.

gloss: An instrument with a magnetic needle that shows direction.

The *compass* needle swung north.
Both *compasses* pointed the same way.
contrast: The first syllable is KUM, not KOM. The same word also names the drawing tool for circles.

gloss: A watch that can be started and stopped to time an event exactly.

gloss: A round face with numbers on it that shows a reading or sets a level.

gloss: A thin metal rod used to check the level of oil in an engine.

gloss: A handheld instrument that measures voltage, current, and resistance.

gloss: An instrument that measures voltage.

gloss: An instrument that measures wind speed.

gloss: An instrument that measures humidity.

gloss: An instrument that records the shaking of the ground during an earthquake.

The lab has a row of *seismographs* along one wall.

gloss: An open container marked with a scale for measuring rainfall.

gloss: Equipment that finds the position and speed of objects using radio waves.

gloss: A device that detects and measures something such as heat, light, or motion.

gloss: The figures shown on the display of an instrument.

gloss: A cup marked with a scale for measuring ingredients.

gloss: A straight-sided glass container marked with a scale, used in laboratories.

gloss: A tall narrow lab container marked for measuring the volume of a liquid.

gloss: The unit of power, used for the output of a bulb, speaker, or motor.

gloss: One thousand watts.

gloss: The unit electricity is sold in, equal to one kilowatt used for one hour.

gloss: The amount of electric power something uses or produces, stated in watts.

gloss: The unit of electrical pressure.

The battery puts out twelve *volts*.
Nine *volts* isn't enough for that motor.

gloss: The electrical force in a circuit, measured in volts.
examples: Check the *voltage* before you plug it in.
Low *voltage* made the lights flicker.
European *voltage* is twice ours.

gloss: A unit of electric current, short for ampere.
examples: That circuit is rated for fifteen *amps*.
The motor pulls about six *amps*.
The breaker trips at twenty *amps*.
contrast: Amp is also short for amplifier, as in a guitar amp.

gloss: The full name of the unit of electric current.
examples: The label gives the current in *amperes*.
One *ampere* is a lot of current for a thin wire.
Fuses are rated in *amperes*.
contrast: In everyday American speech almost everyone says amp instead.

gloss: The unit of electrical resistance.
examples: The resistor is rated at 100 *ohms*.
Measure the resistance in *ohms*.
A few *ohms* won't matter here.

gloss: A unit of engine power equal to 746 watts.
examples: The engine puts out 300 *horsepower*.
That mower doesn't have much *horsepower*.
They compared the *horsepower* of both trucks.
contrast: It stays horsepower after a number, never horsepowers.

gloss: The metric unit of energy or work.
examples: The reaction released 500 *joules*.
One *joule* is a very small amount of energy.
Convert the calories into *joules*.
contrast: Pronounced JOOL, exactly like jewel.

gloss: The unit used to measure how loud a sound is.
examples: A normal conversation is about sixty *decibels*.
Hearing damage starts around 85 *decibels*.
The meter reads in *decibels*.

gloss: The unit of frequency, equal to one cycle per second.
examples: American power runs at sixty *hertz*.
The monitor refreshes at 120 *hertz*.
People hear sound from about 20 *hertz* upward.
contrast: The plural is hertz, and the word sounds like hurts.

gloss: The number of times something repeats in a given period.
examples: The station broadcasts on a low *frequency*.
Raise the *frequency* of the readings to once a minute.
Different *frequencies* travel different distances.

gloss: The metric unit of force.
examples: The spring pulls with a force of ten *newtons*.
One *newton* is about the weight of an apple.
Convert the pounds into *newtons*.
contrast: Americans say NOO-tuhn; the British add a y sound, NYOO-tuhn.

gloss: The turning force produced by an engine or applied to a bolt.
examples: Diesel engines make a lot of *torque*.
Tighten the lug nuts to the right *torque*.
The wrench measures *torque* in foot-pounds.
contrast: The que is a plain k sound: TORK.

gloss: The distance between one wave crest and the next.
examples: Red light has a longer *wavelength* than blue.
The antenna is cut to a quarter *wavelength*.
Only certain *wavelengths* pass through the filter.

gloss: The unit that measures how much visible light a lamp gives off.
examples: This bulb puts out 800 *lumens*.
Flashlights are rated in *lumens* now.
A few hundred *lumens* is plenty for a desk lamp.

gloss: A rating showing how well gasoline resists knocking in an engine.
examples: The manual calls for 91 *octane*.
Higher *octane* costs more per gallon.
Regular gas is 87 *octane* in most states.

gloss: The distance north or south of the equator, measured in degrees.
examples: Chicago sits at about 42 degrees *latitude*.
Enter the *latitude* and longitude.
Northern *latitudes* get very little winter sun.
contrast: Americans say LAT-uh-tood; the British say LAT-i-tyood.

gloss: The distance east or west of the prime meridian, measured in degrees.
examples: The ship radioed in its *longitude*.
Lines of *longitude* meet at the poles.
Two cities at the same *longitude* can have very different weather.
contrast: The g is a j sound: LAHN-juh-tood.

gloss: Height above sea level.
examples: Denver sits at an *elevation* of about a mile.
The trail gains 2,000 feet of *elevation*.
Water boils sooner at high *elevations*.

gloss: The average level of the ocean's surface, used as the zero point for heights.
examples: The town is 300 feet above *sea level*.
*Sea level* has risen several inches in a century.
Baking times change well above *sea level*.

gloss: The space between two lines that meet, measured in degrees.
examples: Cut the trim at a 45-degree *angle*.
Measure the *angle* with a protractor.
All three *angles* add up to 180 degrees.

gloss: One of a set of numbers giving an exact position.
examples: Send me the *coordinates* and I'll find it.
Each *coordinate* is given in degrees.
The GPS *coordinates* were off by a block.
contrast: The noun ends in -nut; the verb to coordinate ends in -nayt.

gloss: One long step, or the distance covered by it.
examples: He crossed the room in three *strides*.
The runner's *stride* got shorter near the end.
Long *strides* eat up the distance.

gloss: The inside diameter of a gun barrel.
examples: The rifle is a .22 *caliber*.
Police recovered a bullet of the same *caliber*.
The shop stocks several *calibers*.
contrast: Americans spell it caliber; the British write calibre.

gloss: The hollow inside of a tube or a gun barrel, or the width of it.
examples: The engine has a four-inch *bore*.
Clean the *bore* after every trip to the range.
The two cylinders have identical *bores*.
contrast: Sounds the same as boar, a wild pig, and as bore, the past tense of bear.

gloss: A single item or amount taken for testing or study.
examples: The lab needs a urine *specimen*.
Each *specimen* is labeled and dated.
Museum *specimens* are kept behind glass.
contrast: The stress is on the first syllable: SPES-uh-muhn.

gloss: The weight of the contents alone, without the packaging.
examples: The *net weight* is printed on the side of the box.
The *net weight* is twelve ounces.
Compare the *net weights*, not the package sizes.

gloss: The changing of a measurement from one unit into another.
examples: The chart gives the *conversion* from inches to centimeters.
Do the *conversion* before you order the parts.
Unit *conversions* trip up a lot of students.
